headline: Ritholtz advocates a regret-minimisation framework for concentrated positions — selling enough to lock in life-changing wealth while retaining upside exposure
reasoning: Ritholtz describes a framework for handling concentrated positions such as stock options, crypto, or single-stock windfalls: rather than trying to maximise returns from an unknowable future, investors should ask what decision they would least regret in either outcome — the stock rising or falling. He illustrates with two cases: a 1990s Yahoo stock scenario where selling the first vesting tranche provided life-changing money while retaining two-thirds upside, and a UPS driver with $40 million in Bitcoin where selling half eliminated the worst-case regret while preserving meaningful upside. The goal is to avoid looking back with regret, not to maximise terminal wealth.
quote: Rather than think in terms of how do I maximize my return, which is really going to be dependent on an inherently unknowable future path, instead think about, hey, how am I going to minimize the sort of regrets I have later in life when I look back and say, oh, I would have could have should have done this... So just selling half check the boxes. If you sell 20 million, pay your taxes, pay for your kids' college, pay for your mortgage, go on a really nice vacation... $20 million is a lot of money and now you still have a chunk that if it goes up or down, it doesn't matter, you've already changed the quality of your life. The goal isn't to max out the returns.

He extends this to financial planning, warning that complex personal situations — multiple properties, businesses, inheritances — are poorly served by AI.

headline: Ritholtz argues long-term investors should pre-program buy orders at market drawdowns of 20-50% to overcome emotional selling at bottoms
reasoning: Barry Ritholtz argues that market bottoms are identifiable as capitulatory events but nearly impossible to act on emotionally because every instinct drives investors to sell with the crowd. He recommends pre-programming good-till-cancel limit orders at levels 20-50% below current prices so that the decision is made rationally in advance rather than in the heat of the moment. He notes investors repeatedly regret not buying more in March 2009, March 2020, and October 2022, and that pre-programming removes the emotional barrier. He also warns that market timing requires being right twice — on entry and exit — and most investors are wrong on both sides.
quote: Go back to 08-09, right? The market peaked October 07. Started rolling over in 08, fell like 38%, I'm guessing in 08, the S&P 500. And then the next leg down in 09, right into March, was just pure panic selling. And the old joke is markets bottom on bad news. So if you're waiting for the all clear sign, it's too late. So the solution is to say, I don't know when this is going to bottom, but I'm a long-term investor and down 20, down 30, down 40%, down 50%, I'm a buyer. So here's some cash and I'm willing to pre-programmed already there. Put this in.

The lesson is that identifying a great stock is difficult, but knowing when to hold versus when to sell is equally or more challenging.

headline: Gold serves as a store of value and hedge against extreme tail-risk scenarios, not a routine inflation hedge, with long-run returns roughly tracking inflation.
reasoning: Roger Aliaga Diaz argues that gold's primary role is as a hedge against extreme scenarios such as U.S. dollar debasement or a fiscal crisis, rather than as a hedge against ordinary inflation shocks. Over 100 years of data, gold's returns have roughly kept pace with inflation, but performance is highly time-period dependent — for example, 2013 delivered only 1.1% return. As long as the U.S. dollar remains the global reserve currency, flight-to-safety flows go to the dollar; gold becomes relevant only if confidence in the dollar erodes and no other currency is ready to replace it. He sees gold as a commodity with no income generation, so its value is purely determined by supply and demand and future price expectations.
quote: There is a store of value type of role of gold, which I completely agree with. I mean, if you see over 100 years of data, you will see that the return for gold has been keeping track with inflation, sometimes even ahead. Of course, it's a very time period dependent, right? There are periods in which, okay, if you're in the 70s, you get like 20% per year. But even the last 14, 15 years, as much as we are looking at the gold prices today, the returns in 2013 is 1.1%, right? So I think gold over time on average keeps track of inflation, preserves value. And that certainly is a role that sometimes people think. Gold to me is a hedge against more extreme scenarios. Not the regular garden variety, inflation shocks.
